CHAPTER XXI

Speech is the familiar vent of human thoughts; but there are emotions so
simple and overpowering, that they rush out not in words, but eloquent
sounds. At such moments man seems to lose his characteristics, and to
be merely one of the higher animals; for these, when greatly agitated,
ejaculate, though they cannot speak.

There was something terrible and truly animal, both in the roar
of triumph with which the pursuers burst out of the thicket on our
fugitives, and the sharp cry of terror with which these latter darted
away. The pursuers hands clutched the empty air, scarce two feet behind
them, as they fled for life. Confused for a moment, like lions that miss
their spring, Dierich and his men let Gerard and the mule put ten yards
between them. Then they flew after with uplifted weapons. They were
sure of catching them; for this was not the first time the parties had
measured speed. In the open ground they had gained visibly on the three
this morning, and now, at last, it was a fair race again, to be settled
by speed alone. A hundred yards were covered in no time. Yet still there
remained these ten yards between the pursuers and the pursued.

This increase of speed since the morning puzzled Dierich Brower. The
reason was this. When three run in company, the pace is that of the
slowest of the three. From Peter's house to the edge of the forest
Gerard ran Margaret's pace; but now he ran his own; for the mule was
fleet, and could have left them all far behind. Moreover, youth and
chaste living began to tell. Daylight grew imperceptibly between the
hunted ones and the hunters. Then Dierich made a desperate effort, and
gained two yards; but in a few seconds Gerard had stolen them quietly
back. The pursuers began to curse.

Martin heard, and his face lighted up. “Courage, Gerard! courage, brave
lad! they are straggling.”

It was so. Dierich was now headed by one of his men, and another dropped
into the rear altogether.

They came to a rising ground, not sharp, but long; and here youth, and
grit, and sober living told more than ever.

Ere he reached the top, Dierich's forty years weighed him down like
forty bullets. “Our cake is dough,” he gasped. “Take him dead, if you
can't alive;” and he left running, and followed at a foot's pace. Jorian
Ketel tailed off next; and then another, and so, one by one, Gerard ran
them all to a standstill, except one who kept on stanch as a bloodhound,
though losing ground every minute. His name, if I am not mistaken,
was Eric Wouverman. Followed by him, they came to a rise in the wood,
shorter, but much steeper than the last.

“Hand on mane!” cried Martin.

Gerard obeyed, and the mule helped him up the hill faster even than he
was running before.

At the sight of this manoeuvre, Dierich's man lost heart, and, being now
full eighty yards behind Gerard, and rather more than that in advance of
his nearest comrade, he pulled up short, and, in obedience to Dierich's
order, took down his crossbow, levelled it deliberately, and just as the
trio were sinking out of sight over the crest of the hill, sent the bolt
whizzing among them.

There was a cry of dismay; and, next moment, as if a thunder-bolt had
fallen on them, they were all lying on the ground, mule and all.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER TWO.
[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"O God! It's all over with me," said he at last. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What's the matter, master?" said I.
[Reference Rewrite]: I left him in the dark, initiating a careful descent down the rain-slicked precipices that formed the carceral walls of our world. Before I had traversed fifty paces, a sudden rupture of lightning tore the sky, pursued instantly by a shriek so guttural it arrested my breath. It was a sound stripped of all former sovereignty. I could not trace its origin through the howling wind, but then I heard the voice—his voice, diminished and frantic—commanding my return.

I obeyed, stepping back over the jagged stone, and found him frozen exactly where I had left him.

"You called me, master?" I asked, testing the word on my tongue.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

Speech is the familiar vent of human thought, yet there exist emotions so primal and overwhelming that they erupt not in articulate words, but in raw, eloquent cries. In such moments, man sheds his civilized veneer, revealing himself as nothing more than a higher beast; for when driven to the brink of agitation, even the most refined creatures reduce themselves to mere ejaculation, stripped of speech. There was something terrifyingly bestial in the triumphant roar that erupted from the thicket as Dierich's men burst forth upon their quarry, mirrored instantly by the piercing shriek of terror that drove Gerard and the mule into flight. The pursuers' hands clawed at the empty air, grasping at ghosts mere feet behind them, as they chased a phantom of survival. For a fleeting second, confused and disoriented like lions that have missed their spring, Dierich and his followers faltered, allowing Gerard and the beast to carve out a ten-yard sanctuary. Then, fueled by adrenaline, they surged forward with weapons raised, certain of capture. This was not the first time these factions had tested their mettle against one another; earlier that morning, in the open fields, they had visibly closed the gap on the trio. Now, however, fate had reset the board for a contest decided solely by velocity.

A hundred yards vanished in the blink of an eye, yet those crucial ten yards persisted, a stubborn barrier between hunter and hunted. This sudden acceleration baffled Dierich Brower. The truth lay in the mechanics of motion itself: when three flee together, their pace is dictated by the slowest link. From Peter's house to the forest's edge, Gerard had been tethered to Margaret's slower stride; now, unburdened by her presence, he ran with his own youthful vigor, aided by a mule capable of leaving the entire party in the dust. Furthermore, the benefits of youth and chastity began to manifest physically. Light began to bleed perceptibly into the space separating the hunted from the hunters. Desperate to close the distance, Dierich made a final, valiant effort, gaining two yards, only for Gerard to steal them back in a heartbeat. The pursuit dissolved into a chorus of curses. Martin heard them, and a spark ignited in his eyes. "Courage, Gerard! Courage, brave lad! They are breaking apart!" And indeed, the formation fractured. Dierich was now led by a single man, while another lagged entirely to the rear.

They ascended a long, gentle rise, and here, the advantages of youth, grit, and sober living proved insurmountable. Before reaching the summit, the weight of Dierich's forty years crushed him, feeling heavier than forty leaden bullets. "Our prey is turning to dough," he gasped, abandoning the sprint to follow at a walking pace. Jorian Ketel trailed off next, followed by others until one by one, Gerard ran them all to a halt, save for a solitary figure who pressed on with the relentless tenacity of a bloodhound, though steadily losing ground. His name, if my memory serves, was Eric Wouverman. Following him, they approached a sharper, steeper rise within the woods. "Hold fast to the mane!" Martin shouted. Gerard obeyed, and the mule propelled him upward with a speed surpassing his previous running. Witnessing this maneuver, Dierich's remaining follower lost his nerve. Now fully eighty yards behind Gerard and significantly ahead of his nearest comrade, he halted abruptly. Obedient to Dierich's silent command, he lowered his crossbow, leveled it with deliberate precision, and just as the trio disappeared over the crest of the hill, released the bolt. It whizzed through the air with deadly intent. A cry of dismay shattered the silence, and the next instant, as if struck by a thunderbolt, they all lay prone upon the earth—the men and the mule alike, silenced by the arrow.
